Blight

/BLYT/ - rhymes with night · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Blight means a disease that destroys growing plants.

A blight reached the island's banana groves in June, and by harvest every plantation on the windward slope stood bare.

Worked Example

Wheat rust is older than the alphabet; Roman farmers held a spring festival just to beg it away from their grain. When a new race of the fungus appeared in Uganda in 1999, breeders watched it defeat one resistant variety after another, and seed banks on five continents began crossing wild grasses in a hurry. A single infected stem can shed enough spores to sicken a whole district.

Blight is the exact word for rust, because a blight is a disease that destroys growing plants — and destroys is the operative claim. Mildew films a leaf's surface and spoils its looks; rot takes the tissue it touches and stops there. A blight travels, jumping plant to plant until whole harvests are gone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

canker: a localized sore on bark or stem; a blight sweeps whole plantings

mildew: a surface fungus that films leaves; a blight kills as it spreads

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bloom: healthy flowering

vigor: strong, healthy growth

Where it sits · how far and fast the damage spreads — mildew → rot → blight

mildew vs. blight: Mildew is the light rung — a gray film that dulls the leaf's surface and rarely kills the plant.

rot vs. blight: Rot goes further than mildew — the tissue it touches dies — but blight claims the most: it races plant to plant and takes the whole field.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — blight

Root — blight: plant-killing disease (origin unknown)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel: blight arrived in farm speech around 1600 as a single, parentless word. Etymologists have guessed at Old English skin-disease terms and Norse cousins, but no line of descent holds up — the name of the crop-killer simply appeared, much the way the thing itself does.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Blight surfaced among English farmers and gardeners around 1600 with no traceable parent — no Latin root, no provable Old English ancestor. It names the destroyer without ever telling you where its own name came from, which somehow suits it.

Strength Check

Word Choice

plain / agricultural, often figurative

Blight is literal in the garden and just as famous in the city — planners speak of urban blight eating a neighborhood the way rust eats wheat. Keep it for harm that spreads through what it kills. A bane (this unit) stands outside its victim and wears it down; a blight is inside, moving. Mildew and canker are its smaller cousins.
